import pytest, semver

def test_triage():
    with pytest.raises(TypeError) as excinfo:
        semver.Version.parse(3.14)
    assert "not expecting type" in str(excinfo.value)
findings.label: semver/version.py:637 in Version.parse: `%` -> `*` (arithmetic)
findings.why: `'...%s' % type` becomes `'...%s' * type`. Both raise TypeError, so a bare pytest.raises(TypeError) cannot tell them apart — but the message differs, so asserting it does.

import semver

def test_triage():
    assert str(semver.Version.parse("1.2.3").bump_build(token="")) == "1.2.3+1"
    assert str(semver.Version.parse("1.2.3").bump_build(token="x")) == "1.2.3+x.1"
findings.label: semver/version.py:355 in Version.bump_build: `==` -> `!=` (equality)
findings.why: EQUIVALENT — the mutated line is in DEAD CODE. In semver 3.0.4, `bump_build` computes `build`, increments it, then recomputes the identical if/elif chain and increments again, discarding the first result entirely. The mutant sits in that discarded first block, so no input can distinguish it. Mutation testing surfaced an upstream redundancy that 100% coverage did not. (The expected value below, '1.2.3+1', was obtained from the oracle rather than guessed — the author's first hand-written guess of '1.2.3+0' was wrong, which is precisely the failure mode Placebo removes from the agent.)

findings.label: semver/version.py:598 in Version.match: `0` -> `1` (constant)
findings.why: ">=": (0, 1) -> (1, 1) drops equality, so ">=x" stops matching x.

    b = semver.Version.parse("0.2.0")
    assert a.is_compatible(b) is False
findings.label: semver/version.py:730 in Version.is_compatible: `False` -> `None` (return_value)
findings.why: `return False` -> `return None`. None is falsy, so every truthiness use is unaffected. Only an identity/equality assertion on the return value can see it.
